title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
purpose: It compiles the Ismaili legal rulings, drawn from named books and from the author's own correspondence with his teachers, governing the washing, shrouding, perfuming, carrying, praying over, and burying of the dead.

points.text: The washing of the dead requires the ablution performed three times together with three washings, though performing the ablution at the last washing suffices, as stated in the Book of Reports.

Where water is scarce, the answer given is that a living man in janabah uses the water and the dead is given tayammum with earth; another report permits a washer in janabah to wash the dead, performing tayammum first if washing would harm him, when no one else can be found.

A martyr is normally not washed, but the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif rules that a martyr who was in janabah is washed on account of that janabah, and one found dead with no mark upon him is washed, given hanut, and shrouded.

The Mukhtasar al-Athar rules that the drowned and the burned are washed, as is any severed limb whose separation would preclude life, each detached limb being washed and set in its own place before shrouding; no hair is shaved and no nail trimmed from the dead.

Answering the author's question from Hind, Jafar ibn Sulayman rejects the wrapper arrangement used by the Daudi group and by unbelievers, ruling that the Pillars prescribes only an izar from navel to knee with water passed beneath it and the washer's cloth-wrapped hand reaching under it, while conceding that a screen is the better course, especially for a woman.
The best shroud, per Jafar ibn Muhammad in The Pillars of Islam, is three garments: a shirt neither buttoned nor hemmed, a wrapping sheet, and a waist wrapper.

Al-Qadi al-Numan's term 'tajir' for a woman's shrouding is defined as gathering the shirt at the navel down over the clothing and tucking it into the izar's fastening — a mark distinguishing women from men, like the head covering.

Ali's counsel that whoever touches the body of the dead after it has grown cold must perform the washing is glossed as meaning after his end has come and he has been washed according to the sunnah, since the dead body has become impure and its moisture renders a living man impure.

For conjoined twins, the summoners of Yemen rule that separation is done only if slight and safe; if dangerous they are left, their life and death counting as one, and if one dies the adhering part is cut from the dead one only where the living feels no pain.
The shroud and outfitting are taken from the estate first — before debt and bequest — according to the deceased's station even if costly and even if the debt exceeds the estate.

Hanut is any perfume placed on the places of prostration and named parts of the body, but wars and saffron are excluded for men and included for women; the dead himself is not incensed — only his shroud and the place of washing — and Ali forbids any fragrance but camphor since the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage.
One who dies in a state of pilgrim consecration has his head and face left uncovered and no perfume brought near him, because he remains consecrated during days that are numbered.

Walking before the bier is disliked only for an enemy of the family because angels of wrath attend it; for believers, encompassed by angels of mercy, position does not matter though walking behind is more excellent, and the call to prayer at the bier is disliked while announcing the death without a public call is permitted.
The Prophet turned back women following a bier, telling them they neither pray over it, carry it, lower it, nor cover it, and so should return excused but unrewarded.

The funeral prayer is a communal obligation on every Muslim who knows of it until one performs it, may be offered anywhere and even in disliked hours or at an eclipse, and the supplication between takbirs may be recited or left to the imam.

In the absence of the imam of the age, the right to lead the funeral prayer belongs first to his appointed judge or officeholder, then to the highest in station among those the imam has advanced, then to the appointed prayer leader, and only if none is present to the most entitled guardian.

The funeral prayer is offered over martyrs, grave sinners, those executed under prescribed punishment or retaliation, and even one who has taken his own life; the supplication is quiet by day and aloud by night.
The dead is buried in the burial ground of the town where he died and not carried to another, unless he dies in open wilderness, in which case he may be carried to the nearest burial ground.
Burial in another's land requires his leave, but once done without consent the owner may claim only the value of the grave sites and may not have the bodies removed.

Baked brick, stone, and whatever else is available may be placed over the dead, contrary to the dislike of it held by the people of the outward sense, and the questioner is told to rely on this except where prudent concealment requires otherwise.

Ali counsels visiting the graves of those who have a claim upon one and seeking provision there, since the dead rejoice at such visits, and a man should ask his need at his parents' graves after praying for them.
